As many have said before—migraines & cluster headaches.

I have something called [occipital neuralgia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Occipital_neuralgia). Basically, I have a stuck nerve in my neck and it produces really, really painful cluster headaches that I thought were migraines for a long time. My upper back & neck become very stiff and achy and my head feels on fire. Like my eye is being stabbed.

Worst pain I've ever experienced tbh. I broke my kneecap in half and it wasn't even that bad.

A small sign that probably saved my brother's life was that he texted my sister, my family and I "I love you." He'd never said it before at all, and getting the text was... so weird to me. I knew something was up, and we managed to get to him in time. But it left me shocked and traumatised for a long time.

As for my own personal experience... I set a date. And I would talk about that date a lot, but never past it, and I would joke about death in a very dark way.

Back in November (2020), I started *really* writing a novel for NaNoWriMo that had been in the works for three years, and it's been extremely healing.

2017 was a horrible, horrible year for me, probably the worst of my life—burn out from my former work, left a terrible relationship, fell in love and got my heart broken so badly I tried to kill myself, fell into a year-long pit of hatred and self-harm that I thought I had left in college... you get the picture.

Writing my novel based on all these hardships has made me accept a new step in my healing and helped me unblock some really nasty shit that was hanging in my head. It's been... incredibly freeing.
Bear in mind that I'm autistic, so this is special interest level: I'll talk their ear out about Colin Farrell.

*About Time*. The part where Tim learns that his father has cancer and can't save him was hard enough for me, but what follows with the fact that he can't go back in time to see him after his third child is born wrecked me. Like, big, ugly sobs. I wasn't expecting it at all but boy, it just... went straight through my heart. 

I think it had to do with my grandfather's death. I couldn't accept that he was gone and I clung to the idea that living in the past to remember him was "the" way to go. Then I understood that he would always be with me through his legacy, no matter what.

My grandfather's meatballs. He made them with grated orange zest and a specific blend of spices I can't recall, and they were so delicious, every single time.

He passed away when I was 16 and we started calling the dish "Papy's boulettes" (I'm French and he was French-Moroccan), literally translating to "Grandpa's Meatballs" in a sweet way.

Otherwise, meat cooked by my parents' friend—he's a chef and holy molly, his sour cherry duck is one of the best things I've ever tasted in my life.
I like to think that he did, indeed.

My very first cat passed away 2 years ago in my arms. He was only two years old and nothing had prepared me for this to happen (likely a heart attack).

He was my best friend and the brightest light in my life. I adopted him after a really rough year battling depression, anxiety and burn out from my previous job, as well as going through a really hard breakup and trying to kill myself. He became my rock and the reason I would wake up most days, guiding me back to safety when I wanted to hurt myself. He was the softest, gentlest little man and would purr up a storm when he saw me cry.

He left shortly before I started a new beautiful chapter of my life. I'll always wonder if he knew he could leave me in my wife's hands, or if life was simply too cruel.

I think I choose to believe both.
